title: Plante v. Jacobs
lead: Frank and Carol Jacobs withheld the balance on their new house because of missing work and defects, including a living room narrowed by a misplaced wall. Their builder sought the unpaid price, leaving the courts to decide whether the house substantially performed the contract and how each defect should be valued.

actors.name: Eugene Plante
actors.role: Builder who supplied materials and constructed the house.

actors.name: Frank and Carol Jacobs
actors.role: Homeowners who disputed completion and workmanship.

actors.name: Justice Hallows
actors.role: Author of the Wisconsin Supreme Court opinion.

proceedings: The trial court found substantial performance and deducted allowances for established omissions and defects, while denying disputed extras. The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed on the owners’ appeal and the builder’s review requests. Rehearing was later denied.
limits: The account distinguishes the assigned introduction’s transaction facts from the judicial opinion’s findings and analysis. No exact final net recovery is supplied. The living-room-wall ruling depends on the particular evidence of destructive repair and no market-value loss, not a universal rejection of personal contractual purposes.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A house contract breaks down over completion and workmanship
paragraphs: Eugene Plante agreed to furnish materials and build a house for Frank and Carol Jacobs on their Brookfield lot for $26,765. The homeowners paid $20,000 before disputes over workmanship and completion led them to withhold further payment. Plante did not finish and sought a lien for the unpaid balance and claimed extras; the owners asserted deficient and incomplete work.

Plante conceded missing kitchen cabinets, gutters and downspouts, a sidewalk, closet clothes poles, and an entrance seat, totaling $1,601.95. The trial court credited that amount to the owners. They asserted approximately twenty more defects and contended that complete correction would cost twenty-five to thirty percent of the contract price.

sections.title: A misplaced wall creates the largest disputed repair
sections.cue: What did the trial court do with the competing claims?
paragraphs: The owners’ principal objection concerned an interior wall that reduced the living room’s width by more than a foot. Moving it would cost about $4,000. The house had been finished and decorated around the wall, and the Jacobs family occupied it. Experts on both sides agreed that the narrower room did not reduce market price.

The trial court found substantial performance and allowed the builder recovery subject to deductions for established deficiencies. The homeowners appealed, seeking $10,000 in damages. Plante sought review of the denial of claimed extras and the allowance for reconstructing a patio wall, arguing for only $650 in damages. The Supreme Court had to evaluate the differentiated treatment of the defects rather than simply choose one party’s total.

sections.title: Substantial performance turns on the promised purpose
sections.cue: Why did numerous defects not necessarily bar recovery on the contract?
paragraphs: Justice Hallows explained that contract recovery required substantial performance; otherwise the builder would at most have a claim for the reasonable value of services. Substantial performance depended on fulfilling the agreement’s essential purpose, not a mathematical percentage of completion or repair cost.

A building need not perfectly match every specification unless the parties made particular details essential. A feature with special or great personal importance could still prevent substantial performance if omitted. The Court’s earlier cases concerning a grossly inadequate boiler, a practically useless boathouse, defective painting, or a heating system failing its intended function illustrated failures of essential purpose.

This house was built from a stock floor plan rather than detailed blueprints, with standard-form specifications modified and supplemented by the parties. Practical construction experience supplied many details. The owners received a usable house despite numerous dissatisfactions, and the record did not establish that every detail was essential. Their proposed repair-cost percentage therefore did not defeat substantial performance.

sections.title: Different defects can call for different measures of loss
sections.cue: Why did several correction allowances stand?
paragraphs: With substantial performance, the builder could recover the contract price less damage from incomplete or defective work. Diminution in value compared the house delivered with the house promised. Repair cost could help show that loss but did not necessarily equal it.

Small, separable defects could be valued by reasonable correction costs when repairs did not destroy substantial completed work. Where separating defects would cause confusion, diminution could apply collectively. The nature and scale of each defect mattered, and unreasonable economic waste limited destructive reconstruction.

Here the defects could be separated without confusion. The trial judge had rejected unproved items, and those findings were not against the great weight and clear preponderance of the evidence. Repairing ceiling-plaster cracks, mud jacking and fixing the patio floor, and rebuilding a nonstructural patio wall did not involve unreasonable waste in relation to the house and its cost. Those allowances remained in place.

sections.title: Rebuilding the living-room wall would destroy substantial finished work
sections.cue: Why did the owners receive no recovery for that defect?
paragraphs: Moving the wall would damage other parts of the house and require replastering and redecorating walls and ceilings in at least two rooms. There was no showing that the owners demanded relocation while construction was underway.

The applicable diminution measure therefore contemplated leaving the wall where it stood. Because both sides’ experts agreed that its placement did not affect market price, the owners proved no recoverable loss for this defect. Their preference for the specified room dimensions remained unsatisfied, but the destructive repair cost did not establish the proper recovery on these facts. The Court’s recognition that specially important contractual features can matter kept this result from becoming a categorical rule against personal purposes.

sections.title: The builder also fails to establish the disputed extras
paragraphs: The contract required written agreement for extra work, and no such writing existed. Evidence conflicted over whether the work was actually extra and whether the owners waived the writing requirement. Plante bore the burden and did not show error in denying those claims. His objection to the patio-wall allowance failed under the same reasonable-repair analysis applied to the owners’ appeal.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the judgment, including substantial performance, the supported defect allowances, no recovery for relocating the living-room wall, and denial of the disputed extras. The report identifies no separate judicial writing or numerical vote. It records denial of rehearing on October 4, 1960, with $25 costs.
